claim: Bacterial flagella are extracellular filaments that drive swimming in bacteria.
source: Bacterial ﬂagella are extracellular ﬁlaments that drive swimming in bacteria.
evidence: This is established scientific knowledge about bacterial flagella function.

claim: During motor assembly, flagellins are transported unfolded through the central channel in the flagellum to the growing tip.
source: During motor assembly, ﬂagellins are transported unfolded through the central channel in the ﬂagellum to the growing tip.
evidence: This is established knowledge about flagellar assembly mechanism.

claim: The flagellar growth rate of Vibrio alginolyticus is initially constant at 50 nm/min when the flagellum is shorter than 1500 nm.
source: Initially, the ﬂagellum grows at a constant rate (50 nm/min) when shorter than 1500 nm.
evidence: This is directly measured from experimental data shown in Figure 2c.

claim: The flagellar growth rate decays sharply when the flagellum grows longer than 1500 nm, decreasing to ~9 nm/min at 7500 nm.
source: The growth rate decays sharply when the ﬂagellum grows longer, which decreases to ~9 nm/min at 7500 nm.
evidence: This is directly measured from experimental data shown in Figure 2c.

claim: When the flagellum is short, its growth rate is determined by the loading speed at the base.
source: When the ﬂagellum is short, its growth rate is determined by the loading speed at the base.
evidence: This is a conclusion from the mathematical model fitting to experimental data.

claim: When the flagellum grows longer, diffusion of flagellin becomes the rate-limiting step, dramatically reducing the growth rate.
source: Only when the ﬂagellum grows longer does diffusion of ﬂagellin become the rate-limiting step, dramatically reducing the growth rate.
evidence: This is a conclusion from the mathematical model fitting to experimental data.

claim: Most bacteria swim by rotating their flagella in aqueous solutions.
source: In aqueous solutions, most bacteria swim by rotating their flagella (Berg, 2003; Sowa and Berry, 2008).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: The bacterial flagellar motor uses the transmembrane electrochemical proton motive force (PMF) to power rotation.
source: Using the transmembrane electrochemical proton motive force (PMF) to power the bacterial flagellar motor (BFM) (Manson et al., 1977; Gabel and Berg, 2003), fast rotating flagella can propel their cell body at a speed of 15–100 μm/s (Xue et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: Fast rotating flagella can propel bacterial cell bodies at speeds of 15–100 μm/s.
source: Using the transmembrane electrochemical proton motive force (PMF) to power the bacterial flagellar motor (BFM) (Manson et al., 1977; Gabel and Berg, 2003), fast rotating flagella can propel their cell body at a speed of 15–100 μm/s (Xue et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous research.

claim: Bacterial flagella are usually about 3–10 times the length of the cell body.
source: Bacterial flagella, usually about 3–10 times the length of the cell body, are hollow protein cylinders of 20 nm outer diameter and 2 nm inner diameter (Yonekura et al., 2003).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous research.

claim: Bacterial flagella are hollow protein cylinders of 20 nm outer diameter and 2 nm inner diameter.
source: Bacterial flagella, usually about 3–10 times the length of the cell body, are hollow protein cylinders of 20 nm outer diameter and 2 nm inner diameter (Yonekura et al., 2003).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous research.

claim: Bacterial flagella are self-assembled from thousands of flagellin monomers.
source: This long extracellular organelle is self-assembled from thousands of flagellin monomers (Figure 1a) (Yonekura et al., 2003; Asakura, 1970).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous research and illustrated in Figure 1a.

claim: The flagellum assembles from the inside out, beginning with the basal body of the BFM.
source: Previous research has established that the flagellum assembles from the inside out, beginning with the basal body of the BFM, after which a type III flagellar secretion system (T3FSS) attaches to the base of this basal body (Macnab, 2003; Minamino et al., 2008; Chevance and Hughes, 2008).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: A type III flagellar secretion system (T3FSS) attaches to the base of the basal body after the basal body forms.
source: Previous research has established that the flagellum assembles from the inside out, beginning with the basal body of the BFM, after which a type III flagellar secretion system (T3FSS) attaches to the base of this basal body (Macnab, 2003; Minamino et al., 2008; Chevance and Hughes, 2008).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: The T3FSS utilizes energy derived from ATP hydrolysis and PMF to unfold and deliver flagellin.
source: Utilizing energy derived from ATP hydrolysis and PMF (Paul et al., 2008; Minamino and Namba, 2008; Lee and Rietsch, 2015), the T3FSS continuously unfolds and delivers flagellin to the hollow interior of the motor, whereupon each unfolded flagellin protein is transported to the end of the filament and there polymerizes to extend the structure (Chevance and Hughes, 2008; Galán et al., 2014; Diepold and Armitage, 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: Each unfolded flagellin protein is transported to the end of the filament and polymerizes to extend the structure.
source: Utilizing energy derived from ATP hydrolysis and PMF (Paul et al., 2008; Minamino and Namba, 2008; Lee and Rietsch, 2015), the T3FSS continuously unfolds and delivers flagellin to the hollow interior of the motor, whereupon each unfolded flagellin protein is transported to the end of the filament and there polymerizes to extend the structure (Chevance and Hughes, 2008; Galán et al., 2014; Diepold and Armitage, 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: Iino (1974) reported that the flagellar growth rate of Salmonella typhimurium decays exponentially with its length.
source: In 1974, Iino (Iino, 1974) used electron microscopy to observe the lengths of Salmonella typhimurium flagella in different growth phases and reported that the flagellar growth rate decays exponentially with its length.
evidence: This is a citation to previous research findings.

claim: Aizawa and Kubori (1998) confirmed that flagellar growth rate decays exponentially with length in Salmonella typhimurium.
source: Later, Aizawa and Kubori (1998) used dark-field microscopy to measure the bacterial flagellar length distribution at different time points and confirmed the same result.
evidence: This is a citation to previous research findings.

claim: Turner et al. (2000, 2012) found that the average flagellar growth rate in Escherichia coli is a constant value independent of the flagellar length.
source: In contrast, more recently, (Turner et al., 2000, 2012) labeled Escherichia coli's pre-existing and newly grown flagellar segments with fluorescent dyes of two different colors and found that the average flagellar growth rate is a constant value independent of the flagellar length.
evidence: This is a citation to previous research findings.

claim: Nearly all existing experimental investigations of flagellar growth have been based on population measurements at two different time points at long intervals.
source: Despite this controversy, nearly all existing experimental investigations have been based on population measurements of flagellar length at two different time points at long intervals.
evidence: This is a characterization of the state of the field based on knowledge of previous research.

claim: Vibrio alginolyticus has only one polar flagellum.
source: To overcome these difficulties, we used V. alginolyticus as our experimental system, which has several advantages: (1) V. alginolyticus has only one polar flagellum (Furuno et al., 1997; Zhu et al., 2013), thus reducing flagella entangling and making it easier to track
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: The polar flagellum of V. alginolyticus is covered by sheath.
source: (2) The polar flagellum is covered by sheath, which is believed to be a membrane-like structure that contains proteins, lipids and lipopolysaccharide and is contiguous with the outer membrane (McCarter, 2001).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous research.

claim: The sheath is a membrane-like structure that contains proteins, lipids and lipopolysaccharide and is contiguous with the outer membrane.
source: (2) The polar flagellum is covered by sheath, which is believed to be a membrane-like structure that contains proteins, lipids and lipopolysaccharide and is contiguous with the outer membrane (McCarter, 2001).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous research.

claim: The growth of sheath and flagellum are synchronized, with the sheath always tightly wrapping the inner flagellum.
source: Previous research (McCarter, 2001; Allen and Baumann, 1971; Glauert et al., 1963) and our TEM studies revealed the synchronized growth of sheath and flagellum, with the sheath always tightly wrapping the inner flagellum (Figure 1c) and Figure 1—figure supplements 1
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous research and by TEM data shown in figures.

claim: The rich lipids constituent in the sheath can be easily labeled by NanoOrange, a hydrophobic domain targeting fluorescent dye.
source: (3). The rich lipids constituent in the sheath can be easily labeled by a hydrophobic domain targeting fluorescent dye, NanoOrange (Grossart et al., 2000).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous research.

claim: NanoOrange is virtually non-fluorescent before binding and increases its fluorescence dramatically after binding to the sheath.
source: NanoOrange is virtually non-fluorescent before binding and increases its fluorescence dramatically after binding to the sheath (Grossart et al., 2000).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous research.

claim: The labeling speed of NanoOrange is very fast (<1 min) and does not influence flagellar growth.
source: (4) The labeling speed of NanoOrange is very fast (<1 min) and does not influence flagellar growth (Figure 1—figure supplement 3), ensuring immediate visualization of newly grown flagellum, which is necessary to measure flagellar growth in real time
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 3.

claim: The sheathed flagellum is prone to attach to the poly-L-lysine coated coverslip surface along with the cell body.
source: 5) Along with the cell body, the sheathed flagellum is prone to attach to the poly-L-lysine coated coverslip surface.
evidence: This is an observation from the experimental procedure.

claim: The average flagellar length of a bacterial population increases with the culturing time.
source: According to a previous study (Iino, 1974) and our observation (Figure 1—figure supplement 2), the average flagellar length of a bacterial population increases with the culturing time.
evidence: This is supported by a citation and experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2.

claim: The initial growth rates are between 37 and 60 nm/min for flagella shorter than 1500 nm.
source: The initial growth rates are between 37 and 60 nm/min for the flagella shorter than 1500 nm.
evidence: This is directly measured from experimental data shown in Figure 2c.

claim: Within the 5-min measurement interval, flagella shorter than 1500 nm can grow 185–300 nm.
source: Within the 5-min measurement interval, the flagella can grow 185–300 nm.
evidence: This is calculated from the measured growth rates.

claim: Ultra-short flagella (<400 nm) are not able to attach to the surface and therefore accurate measurement is difficult.
source: Ultra-short flagella (<400 nm) are not able to attach to the surface and therefore accurate measurement is difficult.
evidence: This is an observation from the experimental procedure.

claim: The growth rate decreases rapidly as the flagellar length increases from ~1500 nm to ~7500 nm.
source: The growth rate decreases rapidly as the flagellar length increases from ~1500 nm to ~7500 nm.
evidence: This is directly measured from experimental data shown in Figure 2c.

claim: The observed decay in flagellar growth rate is not an artifact caused by different measuring intervals and culturing time.
source: Our flagellar growth rate measurement is not sensitive to the chosen time interval since there is a region (between 1000 and 3000 nm) where both our 5 min and 20 min data overlap and agree. This provides assurance that the observed decay in flagellar growth rate is not an artifact caused by different measuring intervals and culturing time.
evidence: This is inferred from the overlap of data collected at different time intervals.

claim: The sharp decay in flagellar growth rate as the flagellar length increases is reproduced in free-moving flagella.
source: We see that although the data points are not many, the sharp decay in flagellar growth rate as the flagellar length increases has been reproduced, confirming our observation of tethered cells.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2.

claim: The observed length-dependent flagellar growth is not an artifact caused by attaching flagella to the surface.
source: To further prove the observed length dependence of flagellar growth rate is not an artifact caused by attaching flagella to the surface, we conducted a similar measurement of V. alginolyticus flagellar growth rate when the flagella are free to move in space.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data from free-moving flagella shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2.

claim: In V. alginolyticus, the flagellar length increases linearly with time when its length is short.
source: In contrast to previous reports of a constant growth rate in E. coli or a monotonically decreasing rate in S. typhimurium (Iino, 1974; Aizawa and Kubori, 1998; Turner et al., 2012), we found that in V. alginolyticus the flagellar length increases linearly with time when its length is short (Figure 3b), which indicates a constant growth rate.
evidence: This is directly observed from experimental data shown in Figure 3b.

claim: When the flagellum grows longer than 1500 nm, the relationship between flagellar length and time deviates from linearity.
source: When the flagellum grows longer than 1500 nm, the relationship between flagellar length and time deviates from linearity (Figure 3b, the red line), showing a decrease in growth rate.
evidence: This is directly observed from experimental data shown in Figure 3b.

claim: This is the first comprehensive report of in vivo real-time recording of V. alginolyticus single flagellar growth.
source: To our knowledge, this is the first comprehensive report of in vivo real-time recording of V. alginolyticus single flagellar growth.
evidence: This is a claim about the novelty of the work based on knowledge of the field.

claim: This is the first in vivo real-time recording of single filament growth, covering the full range of filament lengths.
source: To our knowledge, this is the first in vivo real-time recording of single filament growth, covering the full range of filament lengths.
evidence: This is a claim about the novelty of the work based on knowledge of the field.

claim: The maximum growth rate is estimated as 50 nm/min, which corresponds to transporting 1.7 flagellins per second.
source: According to our experimental data (Figure 2c), when flagella are short, we observed a plateau in growth rate, which is also the maximum possible growth rate of the system. By extrapolation, this maximum growth rate is estimated as 50 nm/min that corresponds to transporting 1.7 flagellins per second.
evidence: This is calculated from experimental data shown in Figure 2c.

claim: The loading speed Sload was experimentally determined as 1.7 Hz.
source: The maximum growth rate also reveals the number of working cycles of the T3FSS. Therefore, Sload was experimentally determined as 1.7 Hz.
evidence: This is calculated from the maximum growth rate measurement.

claim: The best fit of the model to experimental data was found at LS = 12, D = 5000 nm2/s.
source: The best fit was found at LS = 12, D = 5000 nm2/s.
evidence: This is determined by parameter space search and cost function minimization.

claim: In the short flagella regime, the constant flagellar growth rate is supported by the secretion force of the T3FSS and fast diffusion of flagellins across short distances.
source: In the short flagella regime, the constant flagellar growth rate is supported by the secretion force of the T3FSS and fast diffusion of flagellins across short distances.
evidence: This is a conclusion from the mathematical model fitting to experimental data.

claim: At flagella lengths larger than 1500 nm, the rate-limiting effect of flagellins diffusing across a large distance became increasingly prominent, causing many flagellins to jam in the channel and the growth rate dropped rapidly.
source: At flagella lengths larger than 1500 nm, the rate-limiting effect of flagellins diffusing across a large distance became increasingly prominent, causing many flagellins to jam in the channel (hence the high channel occupancy) and the growth rate dropped rapidly.
evidence: This is a conclusion from the mathematical model fitting to experimental data.

claim: The sheath forms very compact and organized structure, always wrapping the inner flagellum.
source: From the TEM images, we see that sheath forms very compact and organized structure, always wrapping the inner flagellum.
evidence: This is directly observed from TEM images shown in Figure 1c and Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: The exact mechanism driving sheath growth remains a mystery.
source: Although we have experimental evidence to prove the synchronized growth between sheath and flagella, the exact mechanism driving sheath growth remains a mystery.
evidence: This is an acknowledgment of the limits of current knowledge.

claim: A single-file diffusion model without invoking an injection pushing mechanism cannot explain the experimental data.
source: First, the single-file diffusion model without invoking an injection pushing mechanism is a special case of our model when LS = 0. As demonstrated in Figure 4b, to produce a constant flagellar growth rate, the diffusion constant D must be very large to make the loading speed the rate-limiting step. In comparison to our length-dependent flagellar growth data with both a plateau regime and a fast-decay regime, varying D alone is not sufficient to fit the whole curve, as shown in Figure 4d. Therefore, a single-file diffusion model without invoking a push mechanism cannot explain our data.
evidence: This is inferred from model simulations and comparison to experimental data.

claim: The chain mechanism seems difficult to explain the sharp decay in growth rate of V. alginolyticus when its flagellum grows longer.
source: Although this model offers a simple physical mechanism for the constant growth rate, it seems difficult to explain the sharp decay in growth rate of V. alginolyticus when its flagellum grows longer.
evidence: This is inferred from comparing the chain model predictions to experimental observations.

claim: The chain model predicts that flagellar growth is not continuous and that pauses in flagellar growth will be observed at different flagellar lengths.
source: One direct prediction from this mechanism is that flagellar growth is not continuous and that pauses in flagellar growth will be observed at different flagellar lengths.
evidence: This is a logical inference from the chain model mechanism.

claim: Neither a constant growth rate nor pauses in flagellar growth were observed in the experiments.
source: In our experiments, we observed neither a constant growth rate nor pauses in flagellar growth.
evidence: This is directly observed from experimental data.

claim: The experimental data is not explained by the chain model.
source: Therefore, our data is not explained by the chain model.
evidence: This is inferred from the mismatch between chain model predictions and experimental observations.

claim: The loading speed of 1.7 flagellin per second was estimated in V. alginolyticus T3FSS.
source: From the plateau in growth rate when the flagellum is short, we deduce the loading speed of 1.7 flagellin per second of the V. alginolyticus T3FSS.
evidence: This is calculated from experimental data.

claim: The loading of 0.5 flagellin per second was estimated in E. coli by Turner et al.
source: Compared to the results from Turner et al. (Turner et al., 2012; Stern and Berg, 2013), in which the loading of 0.5 flagellin per second was estimated in E. coli, our result is more than three times faster.
evidence: This is a citation to previous research findings.

claim: The loading speed in V. alginolyticus is more than three times faster than in E. coli.
source: Compared to the results from Turner et al. (Turner et al., 2012; Stern and Berg, 2013), in which the loading of 0.5 flagellin per second was estimated in E. coli, our result is more than three times faster.
evidence: This is calculated by comparing the current results to previous findings.

claim: The difference in loading speed is possibly due to the difference between bacterial species.
source: This difference is possibly due to the difference between bacterial species.
evidence: This is speculation about the cause of observed differences.

claim: The V. alginolyticus strain used in this study is VIO5, a lateral flagella deletion strain.
source: The V. alginolyticus strain used in this study is VIO5, a lateral flagella deletion strain (gift from Dr. Michio Homma, Nagoya University, Japan (Furuno et al., 1997).
evidence: This is a description of the experimental materials.

claim: The sheathed flagellum has an over-all diameter of about 300 Å and the inner flagellum is only ~120 Å in diameter.
source: Consistent with the previous study (Glauert et al., 1963), the sheathed flagellum has an over-all diameter of about 300 Å and the inner flagellum is only ~120 Å in diameter.
evidence: This is supported by TEM data and citation to previous research.

claim: Labeling flagellar sheath by NanoOrange is a robust method to quickly visualize the flagellar growth in V. alginolyticus.
source: Therefore, labeling flagellar sheath by NanoOrange is a robust method to quickly visualize the flagellar growth in V. alginolyticus.
evidence: This is concluded from the experimental validation shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: Cells grown in the medium with NanoOrange exhibited identical growth curve to cells in the normal medium.
source: The result showed that cells grown in the medium with NanoOrange exhibited identical growth curve to cells in the normal medium, indicating that labeling by NanoOrange does not affect cell growth
evidence: This is directly observed from experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 3a.

claim: NanoOrange labeling does not affect cell growth.
source: The result showed that cells grown in the medium with NanoOrange exhibited identical growth curve to cells in the normal medium, indicating that labeling by NanoOrange does not affect cell growth
evidence: This is inferred from the identical growth curves shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 3a.

claim: The distributions of flagellar lengths in two culture groups at different incubation times were roughly identical.
source: The distributions of flagellar lengths in two culture groups at different incubation times were roughly identical, demonstrating that NanoOrange labeling does not affect flagellar growth, either.
evidence: This is directly observed from experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 3c.

claim: NanoOrange labeling does not affect flagellar growth.
source: The distributions of flagellar lengths in two culture groups at different incubation times were roughly identical, demonstrating that NanoOrange labeling does not affect flagellar growth, either.
evidence: This is inferred from the identical distributions shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 3c.

claim: The V. alginolyticus flagellin protein FlaE consists of 379 amino acids.
source: The V. alginolyticus flagellin protein FlaE (Uniprot ID D0X0U4) consists of 379 amino acids, which is shorter than the Salmonella enterica flagellin protein FliC of 494 amino acids.
evidence: This is information from a protein database.

claim: The Salmonella enterica flagellin protein FliC consists of 494 amino acids.
source: The V. alginolyticus flagellin protein FlaE (Uniprot ID D0X0U4) consists of 379 amino acids, which is shorter than the Salmonella enterica flagellin protein FliC of 494 amino acids.
evidence: This is information from a protein database.

claim: One turn of 11 flagellins elongates the flagellum by 52 Å in Salmonella enterica.
source: As one turn of 11 flagellins elongates the flagellum by 52 Å in Salmonella enterica (Yonekura et al., 2003), the growth increment of each folded FliC can be estimated as 52 Å/11 = 0.47 nm.
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous research.

claim: The growth increment of each folded FlaE can be estimated as 0.47 nm.
source: Therefore, ΔL of our model (Figure 4), the growth increment of each folded FlaE can be estimated as 0.47 nm.
evidence: This is calculated based on structural similarity to FliC.

claim: The length of the partially unfolded FliC is 74 nm.
source: Given the length of the partially unfolded FliC is 74 nm (Yonekura et al., 2003; Turner et al., 2012) conserved alpha helix, the length of the unfolded FlaE can be estimated as 74×379÷494 = 56 nm.
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: The length of the unfolded FlaE can be estimated as 56 nm.
source: Given the length of the partially unfolded FliC is 74 nm (Yonekura et al., 2003; Turner et al., 2012) conserved alpha helix, the length of the unfolded FlaE can be estimated as 74×379÷494 = 56 nm.
evidence: This is calculated based on the ratio of amino acid lengths.

claim: The FliI ATPase at the core of the T3FSS shares similar molecular structure with the F1 ATPase.
source: Previous research suggests that the FliI ATPase at the core of the T3FSS shares similar molecular structure with the F1 ATPase (Ibuki et al., 2011) that can rotate the central shaft for one revolution by hydrolyzing 3 ATP molecules.
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous research.

claim: The F1 ATPase can rotate the central shaft for one revolution by hydrolyzing 3 ATP molecules.
source: Previous research suggests that the FliI ATPase at the core of the T3FSS shares similar molecular structure with the F1 ATPase (Ibuki et al., 2011) that can rotate the central shaft for one revolution by hydrolyzing 3 ATP molecules.
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous research.

claim: The hypothesized secretion force applied by the apparatus is reasonable and consistent with current knowledge about the system.
source: Although the details of force generation and energy transduction in the T3FSS remain unresolved, from our estimation we see that the hypothesized secretion force applied by the apparatus is reasonable and consistent with our current knowledge about the system.
evidence: This is inferred from energy calculations and comparison to known ATP hydrolysis energetics.

claim: A simple one-dimensional diffusion with a pushing base and an absorbing tip can support flagellar growth and explain its length-dependent features.
source: We see that a simple one-dimensional diffusion with a pushing base and an absorbing tip can support flagellar growth and explain its length-dependent features.
evidence: This is concluded from the mathematical model fitting to experimental data.

claim: The previously reported constant growth rate in E. coli and exponential decay rate in S. typhimurium may correspond to different regimes of a universal length-dependent growth curve.
source: The previously reported constant growth rate in E. coli and exponential decay rate in S. typhimurium may be unique to that bacterial species, or may correspond to different regimes of a universal length-dependent growth curve, similar to the one we reported here.
evidence: This is speculation about how to reconcile different previous findings.

claim: Flagella stained with NanoOrange were morphologically identical to that in the control group.
source: For the NanoOrange group, flagella stained with NanoOrange were morphologically identical to that in the control group, indicating that NanoOrange labeling does not affect flagellar growth nor sheath growth.
evidence: This is directly observed from TEM images shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: Only after formalin fixation do flagella lose their sheath.
source: For the fixation group, we saw the sheath detached from the inner flagellum due to fixation, as previously reported (Glauert et al., 1963). Only after formalin fixation do flagella lose their sheath, which helps us to recognize the two-layered structure of sheath and the core flagellar filament.
evidence: This is directly observed from TEM images and supported by citation.

claim: The flagella of Vibrio alginolyticus are wrapped by sheath and the growth of flagella and sheath are tightly synchronized.
source: By these experiments, we confirmed the flagella of Vibrio alginolyticus are wrapped by sheath and the growth of flagella and sheath are tightly synchronized.
evidence: This is concluded from TEM experiments shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: The V. alginolyticus polar flagellum has a helix radius of 0.16 μm and pitch of 1.5 μm.
source: The fluorescent images of flagella are the 2D projections of the 3D helical filaments with 0.16 μm helix radius and 1.5 μm pitch (Furuno et al., 1997), Figure 2b.
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous research.

claim: The linear fit used for 3D correction is L3D = 1.09 L2D.
source: The linear fit that we used as our correction is L3D = 1.09 L2D.
evidence: This is calculated from the helical geometry as shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1c.

claim: The physical distance corresponding to one pixel is 65 nm in the imaging system.
source: With our imaging system, the physical distance corresponding to one pixel is 65 nm.
evidence: This is a specification of the imaging system.
